import copy
import math
import os
import tempfile

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

OUT_DIR = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="training_curves_")       # figures are written here
BLUE, ORANGE, AQUA, GRAY = "#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a", "#73726c"


def make_data(n, seed):
    """x ~ N(0, I_8) in float32; y = relu(x0 - x1) - relu(x2) + 0.5 * x3 + 0.1 * noise."""
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
    X = torch.randn(n, 8, generator=g)
    clean = torch.relu(X[:, 0] - X[:, 1]) - torch.relu(X[:, 2]) + 0.5 * X[:, 3]
    y = clean + 0.1 * torch.randn(n, generator=g)
    return X, y


def make_model(seed):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    return nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(8, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Dropout(0.2), nn.Linear(64, 1))


X_train, y_train = make_data(1000, seed=0)
X_val, y_val = make_data(1000, seed=1000)

Part 1

Approach. The training loop itself is not hard; what is easy to get wrong is a handful of details:

  • The model's output has shape (B, 1) and the labels have shape (B,). You need squeeze(-1) before subtracting, otherwise it broadcasts to (B, B).
  • Call zero_grad() at every step. PyTorch's backward() adds gradients into .grad; it doesn't overwrite them.
  • evaluate has to switch to eval() mode (turning dropout off), use torch.no_grad() (no computation graph), and restore the original mode afterwards.
  • The training loss is averaged weighted by batch size. Here 1000 is exactly divisible by 50, so weighting makes no difference; it only matters when the last batch is not full.

Each epoch costs one forward and one backward pass, O(n⋅8⋅64).

def evaluate(model, X, y):
    was_training = model.training
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        loss = ((model(X).squeeze(-1) - y) ** 2).mean().item()
    model.train(was_training)
    return loss


def train(model, X_train, y_train, X_val, y_val, lr=0.1, epochs=40, batch_size=50, seed=0):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
    opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=lr)
    n = X_train.shape[0]
    history = {"train": [], "val": [evaluate(model, X_val, y_val)], "train_eval": [evaluate(model, X_train, y_train)]}
    for epoch in range(epochs):
        model.train()
        perm = torch.randperm(n, generator=g)
        total = 0.0
        for start in range(0, n, batch_size):
            idx = perm[start:start + batch_size]
            xb, yb = X_train[idx], y_train[idx]
            opt.zero_grad()
            loss = ((model(xb).squeeze(-1) - yb) ** 2).mean()
            loss.backward()
            opt.step()
            total += loss.item() * len(idx)
        history["train"].append(total / n)
        history["val"].append(evaluate(model, X_val, y_val))
        history["train_eval"].append(evaluate(model, X_train, y_train))
    return history


model = make_model(0)
history = train(model, X_train, y_train, X_val, y_val)

(a) The three reference lines. Let u=x0​−x1​∼N(0,2). For Z∼N(0,s2), E[relu(Z)]=s/2π​ and E[relu(Z)2]=s2/2. The four terms of y use only (x0​,x1​), x2​, x3​, and the noise respectively, so they are independent and their variances simply add:

Var(y)=relu(u)(1−π1​)​​+relu(x2​)(21​−2π1​)​​+0.5x3​41​​​+noise0.01​​=1.76−2π3​≈1.2825.

The best linear model is the projection of y onto the space spanned by {1,x0​,…,x7​}. The inputs used by the different terms are disjoint and independent, so each term can be projected separately. The regression coefficient of relu(u) on u is E[urelu(u)]/E[u2]=(s2/2)/s2=21​, and the coefficient of relu(x2​) on x2​ is likewise 21​. So the best linear model is

y^​=21​(x0​−x1​)−21​x2​+21​x3​+2π​2​−1​,intercept≈0.165.

The variance of the linear part is 41​⋅2+41​+41​=1, and what remains is the linear model's mean squared error: 0.76−2π3​≈0.2825. The noise floor is 0.01; no model's expected error can go below it.

(b) The shape of the validation curve. At initialization the network's outputs are small, so the validation error is roughly E[y2] plus the variance of the random outputs, near or slightly above Var(y) (1.39 with seed=0). After the first epoch it is already down to 0.21, below the linear model's 0.28: the relu network quickly learns the linear part, plus some of the kinks. After that it falls more and more slowly and ends up around 0.020, about twice the noise floor. The validation curve never goes below 0.01.

(c) Why the training curve is always higher. Once plotted, you will see that over the 40 epochs every single point of the training curve is above the validation curve, ending at 0.053 versus 0.020. This is not underfitting, and nothing is wrong with the data. There are two reasons:

  • The training loss is an average over the batches of an epoch, and the model keeps improving during the epoch, so it is higher than the loss at the end of the epoch. This only matters in the first few epochs.
  • The training loss is computed in train() mode, with dropout on; the validation loss is computed in eval() mode. Late in training, almost all of the gap comes from this.

How to measure it: compute the loss on the training set in eval() mode (that is history["train_eval"]); it ends at 0.017, about the same as the validation set's 0.020. So the model performs almost identically on the training and validation sets, and the gap comes from dropout itself.

The exact formula: dropout sits only before the last linear layer. Let the hidden activations be hj​, the last layer's weights wj​, and the masks mj​∼Bernoulli(1−p) independent. Then

fdrop​(x)=b+j∑​wj​hj​1−pmj​​,E[1−pmj​​]=1,Var[1−pmj​​]=1−pp​.

So E[fdrop​]=feval​, and using "squared mean plus variance":

Em​[(fdrop​(x)−y)2]=(feval​(x)−y)2+1−pp​j∑​(wj​hj​)2.

This is an identity: it holds exactly for every sample, with no approximation. The average of the second term on the right over the training set is 0.036 with seed=0, exactly the difference 0.053−0.017 between the last point of the training curve and train_eval.

def dropout_penalty(model, X, p=0.2):
    """p / (1 - p) * mean over samples of sum_j (w_j h_j)^2: the extra loss that dropout adds in expectation."""
    with torch.no_grad():
        h = torch.relu(model[0](X))
        return (p / (1 - p) * ((h * model[3].weight) ** 2).sum(dim=1).mean()).item()


VAR_Y = 1.76 - 3 / (2 * math.pi)                 # 1.2825
LINEAR_MSE = 0.76 - 3 / (2 * math.pi)            # 0.2825
NOISE = 0.01
MEAN_Y = (math.sqrt(2) - 1) / math.sqrt(2 * math.pi)

penalty_train = dropout_penalty(model, X_train)
gap_end = history["train"][-1] - history["train_eval"][-1]

Part 2

The three bugs are listed in the order they show up in the plots. For each one: where it is, what goes wrong, on what input it shows, and how to fix it.

First plot (run as is): the loss never goes down, after a few epochs it climbs faster and faster, and finally becomes nan. With seed=0 the training loss never drops below 1.3 (about as high as Var(y)), climbs to 3.2 in the later epochs, and hits nan at epoch 10. A loss that first fails to fall and then blows up makes the gradient itself the first suspect.

Bug A: no opt.zero_grad() in the loop. loss.backward() adds this step's gradient to .grad, so .grad is the sum of all gradients from the first step until now, and every step moves along this ever-growing sum. Measurement: after two steps, p.grad equals the sum of the two batches' gradients, not the second batch's gradient (the verification code includes this comparison). Mathematically it is exactly equivalent to torch.optim.SGD(momentum=1.0), the heavy-ball method with no damping. Fix: add opt.zero_grad() before backward().

Second plot (A fixed): both curves lie flat on the Var(y) reference line. The training loss sits at 1.32 and validation at 1.26, barely moving over 40 epochs. def train_colleague_fixed(model, X_train, y_train, X_val, y_val, lr=0.1, epochs=40, batch_size=50, seed=0):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
    opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=lr)
    mse = lambda pred, target: ((pred.squeeze(-1) - target) ** 2).mean()   # B: (n, 1) - (n,) broadcasts to (n, n)
    n = X_train.shape[0]
    history = {"train": [], "val": []}
    model.train()
    for epoch in range(epochs):
        perm = torch.randperm(n, generator=g)
        total = 0.0
        for start in range(0, n, batch_size):
            idx = perm[start:start + batch_size]
            opt.zero_grad()                                               # A: backward() adds to .grad
            loss = mse(model(X_train[idx]), y_train[idx])
            loss.backward()
            opt.step()
            total += loss.item() * len(idx)
        history["train"].append(total / n)
        model.eval()                                                      # C: no_grad() does not turn dropout off
        with torch.no_grad():
            history["val"].append(mse(model(X_val), y_val).item())
        model.train()
    return history

The gradient. Let X~=[X, 1] (append a column of ones) and the residual r=X~θ−y. Then L=n1​∥r∥2,

∇L(θ)=n2​X~⊤r,H=∇2L=n2​X~⊤X~.

Note the factor of 2: the loss has no 21​, so the Hessian is 2 times the second-moment matrix of [x,1].

The error of finite differences. Central differences have two kinds of error:

  • Truncation error O(ε2), from the third derivative. L is quadratic, so its third derivative is zero, and the truncation error here is exactly 0; a larger ε does no harm.
  • Rounding error: f itself carries an error of about u∣f∣ (u is the unit roundoff, about 1.1×10−16 for float64 and about 6×10−8 for float32), which dividing by 2ε amplifies to u∣f∣/ε.

At theta0, L≈9 and the gradient norm is about 6, so the relative error is roughly u∣f∣/(ε∥∇L∥)≈1.5u/ε. For float64 with ε=10−6 that is on the order of 10−10 (measured: 3.6×10−10). Autograd and the hand-derived formula compute the same expression and differ only by rounding (measured: on the order of 10−15). For float32 with ε=10−6 the rounding error is amplified to within an order of magnitude of the gradient, and the result is unusable (measured: 0.15). For float32 with ε=10−2 it drops to the order of 10−5 (measured: 2.4×10−5). So gradient checks should be done in float64; for general non-quadratic functions, ε around u1/3 balances the two kinds of error.

def linear_grad(theta, X, y):
    n = X.shape[0]

def fd_grad(f, theta, eps):
    g = torch.zeros_like(theta)
    for i in range(theta.numel()):

        e[i] = eps
        g[i] = (f(theta + e) - f(theta - e)) / (2 * eps)
    return g

The threshold. One step of gradient descent is θt+1​−θ^=(I−ηH)(θt​−θ^). Project the error onto the eigenvectors of H, ai​(t)=ui⊤​(θt​−θ^); each component evolves as its own geometric sequence:

ai​(t)=(1−ηhi​)tai​(0),L(θt​)−L(θ^)=21​(θt​−θ^)⊤H(θt​−θ^)=i∑​21​hi​ai​(t)2.

(b) The theorem. Assume H is positive definite (here X~ has full column rank). Gradient descent with a fixed step size converges to θ^ from any starting point if and only if ∣1−ηhi​∣<1 for all i, i.e.

0<η<η∗=h1​2​=λmax​(H)2​.

At η=η∗, the factor in the h1​ direction is −1: that component flips sign every step while keeping its size, neither converging nor diverging. As long as h1​ is strictly larger than the other eigenvalues, all other components decay.

With seed=0, h1​=2.453 and η∗=0.8153. A common pitfall is forgetting the factor of 2 and writing the threshold as 2/λmax​(X~⊤X~/n). That value is twice the true threshold; the factor in the steepest direction becomes 1−4=−3, and it diverges within a few steps.

Why the eigenvalues of H are all near 2 (κ(H)=1.44): the inputs are independent standard normals plus a column of ones, so X~⊤X~/n≈I9​ and H≈2I. The finite sample spreads the eigenvalues out, over a range of about 2(1±d/n​)2≈[1.64, 2.40] (d=9, n=1000; this is the edge of the Marchenko–Pastur distribution). With seed=0 the measured range is [1.70, 2.45].

(a) The three curves. With η=cη∗, the factor in the steepest direction is 1−2c. In the other directions, since hi​<h1​, the factor is 1−2chi​/h1​.

  • c=0.9: the factor in the steepest direction is −0.8. The factors in the other directions all lie between −0.8 and about −0.25 (since hi​/h1​≥0.69), so they decay faster. So late on each step multiplies the loss by 0.82=0.64: a straight line with slope ln0.64=−0.45, dropping about one order of magnitude every 5 steps, and hitting the rounding floor near 10−16 after seventy or eighty steps.
  • c=1.0: the steepest direction is multiplied by −1 each step, so its share of the loss, 21​h1​a1​(0)2, never changes; all other directions decay. So the curve falls first, then flattens out at 21​h1​a1​(0)2. With seed=0 that value is 0.151, starting from 1.058.
  • c=1.1: the steepest direction is multiplied by −1.2 each step, so the loss is multiplied by 1.44 each step; late on it is a straight line with slope ln1.44=+0.36, reaching the order of 1015 after 100 steps. Directions with hi​>h1​/1.1 also diverge, just more slowly (with seed=0 the second direction is multiplied by −1.02 each step). In the first few steps the curve goes down first, because the error in the other directions is decaying; with seed=0 the minimum is at step 2.

A learning rate only 10% above the threshold turns the loss from "converges fast" to "blows up exponentially." The behavior near the threshold changes abruptly.

(c) reduction="sum". The summed loss is n times the mean, and so are the gradient and the Hessian, so the threshold becomes η∗/n=8.2×10−4. Divide the learning rate by n at the same time and the trajectory is exactly the same as with the mean loss. Conversely, switching to the sum while keeping the learning rate, the factor in the steepest direction is 1−0.9×2×1000=−1799, and it flies off on the first step.

def gd_linear(X, y, lr, steps):
    model = nn.Linear(X.shape[1], 1).to(X.dtype)
    with torch.no_grad():
        model.weight.zero_()
        model.bias.zero_()
    opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=lr)
    thetas = [torch.cat([model.weight.detach().reshape(-1), model.bias.detach()]).clone()]
    for _ in range(steps):
        opt.zero_grad()
        loss = ((model(X).squeeze(-1) - y) ** 2).mean()
        loss.backward()
        opt.step()
        thetas.append(torch.cat([model.weight.detach().reshape(-1), model.bias.detach()]).clone())
    return torch.stack(thetas)

Follow-up questions

1. When fixing bug C, what happens if you add model.eval() but forget to switch back with model.train()? From the second epoch on, dropout stays off, which amounts to training a network without dropout. The training curve falls to 0.012 and ends up below the validation curve; the validation curve ends at 0.017, actually better than Part 1's 0.020. This shows that p=0.2 dropout doesn't help on this task: 1000 samples, a smooth target, and a small network don't overfit much to begin with. Incidentally, after a "fix" like this the history no longer matches Part 1.

2. Why does a missing zero_grad produce nan? It is equivalent to SGD(momentum=1.0). On a quadratic with full batches, each component satisfies at+1​=(2−ηh)at​−at−1​. When 0<ηh<4, the solution is an undamped oscillation:

at​=a0​cos(ω/2)cos(ω(t+21​))​,cosω=1−2ηh​.

Each component's amplitude is ∣a0​∣/1−ηh/4​, slightly larger than its initial value, and it never decays. So the loss oscillates between 0 and slightly above its initial value, neither converging nor diverging. Measured over 2000 full-batch steps, the loss never exceeds 1.1 times its initial value, and even in the last 200 steps it still comes back above half its initial value. With minibatches, the gradient and curvature change at every step, and the undamped oscillation not only fails to die down but gets amplified. The same linear model run for 800 minibatch steps (equivalent to 40 epochs) sees its loss grow by more than a factor of 106. The MLP behaves the same way: in the first plot of Part 2, nan appears at epoch 10.

3. What happens if the training loop's loss is changed to reduction="sum"? The gradient becomes 50 times larger, the effective learning rate goes from 0.1 to 5, and it is nan in the first epoch. Divide the learning rate by 50 and it is exactly the same as before. Only the printed training loss is 50 times larger, and the validation loss (summed over 1000 samples) is 1000 times larger.

4. Can you also do a finite-difference check on the MLP? Yes, but watch three things: use eval() mode, otherwise the two forward passes have different dropout masks and the difference is completely meaningless (measured relative error above 105); use float64; and ReLU has kinks, so any coordinate where ε crosses a kink will be wrong, so check only a few coordinates, or try again at a different random point. Done this way, the relative error is below 10−8.

5. Does 2/λmax​ still hold for the MLP? It is no longer a strict theorem, because the Hessian changes with the parameters; it can only be used locally around the current point. You can estimate λmax​ with Hessian-vector products (double backward) plus power iteration, without building the Hessian. At the end of training, λmax​ of the loss on the full training set in eval mode is about 9.8, giving a local threshold 2/λmax​≈0.20; the learning rate we used, 0.1, is about half of that.

def gd_linear_sum(lr, steps):
    m = nn.Linear(8, 1).double()

        opt.step()
        out.append(torch.cat([m.weight.detach().reshape(-1), m.bias.detach()]).clone())
    return torch.stack(out)

def linear_without_zero_grad(lr, steps, batch_size=None, seed=0):
    m = nn.Linear(8, 1).double()
    with torch.no_grad():
        m.weight.zero_()
        m.bias.zero_()

    for _ in range(steps):

        thetas.append(torch.cat([m.weight.detach().reshape(-1), m.bias.detach()]).clone())
    return torch.stack(thetas)

def top_hessian_eigenvalue(iters, seed):
    gen = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
    v = [torch.randn(p.shape, generator=gen, dtype=torch.float64) for p in params]
    norm = math.sqrt(sum((t ** 2).sum().item() for t in v))
    v = [t / norm for t in v]
    lam = None
    for _ in range(iters):
        hv = torch.autograd.grad(grads, params, grad_outputs=v, retain_graph=True)
        lam = sum((a * b).sum().item() for a, b in zip(hv, v))
        norm = math.sqrt(sum((t ** 2).sum().item() for t in hv))
        v = [t / norm for t in hv]
    return lam
